title: Ἑρμῆς καὶ Καλυψώ
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Dawn rises from beside her husband Tithonus, and the gods gather in council on Olympus. Athena renews her plea for Odysseus, held on Calypso's island, and warns that the suitors now plot to kill his son as well. Zeus reminds her that this homecoming was always the plan, and sends Hermes to tell the nymph that the time has come to release him. Hermes puts on his winged sandals, flies across the sea in the likeness of a gull, and comes to Calypso's wondrous island, where he marvels at her cave, its trees, vine and four springs, before finding Odysseus sitting on the shore in tears, gazing out over the sea he cannot cross. Calypso receives Hermes courteously, seats him on a shining throne, and sets before him a table of ambrosia and red nectar; he eats and drinks while she waits to hear why he has come.

sentences.t:
Ἠὼς δ’ ἐκ λεχέων παρ’ ἀγαυοῦ Τιθωνοῖο
ὤρνυθ’, ἵν’ ἀθανάτοισι φόως φέροι ἠδὲ βροτοῖσιν·
sentences.tr:
Ēōs d’ ek lecheōn par’ agauou Tithōnoio
ōrnyth’, hin’ athanatoisi phoōs pheroi ēde brotoisin·
sentences.l:
And Dawn from her bed, from beside noble Tithonus,
was rising, so that to the immortals she might bring light, and to mortals;
sentences.i: And Dawn rose from her bed beside noble Tithonus, to bring light to the immortals and to mortals alike;
sentences.n: This whole two-line formula opens a new day and is likely to recur at later dawns in the poem. Τιθωνοῖο is a genitive in -οιο; Tithonus was a mortal prince whom Dawn loved and carried off, later granted immortality without eternal youth, so that he withered forever without dying — a myth the line itself does not tell, only assumes. ὤρνυθ’ is an augmented imperfect of ὄρνυμι, 'rouse, rise' (the initial ο lengthens to ω under the temporal augment, giving ὤρνυτο rather than the unaugmented ὄρνυτο); φόως is φῶς uncontracted.

sentences.t:
οἱ δὲ θεοὶ θῶκόνδε καθίζανον, ἐν δ’ ἄρα τοῖσι
Ζεὺς ὑψιβρεμέτης, οὗ τε κράτος ἐστὶ μέγιστον.
sentences.tr:
hoi de theoi thōkonde kathizanon, en d’ ara toisi
Zeus hypsibremetēs, hou te kratos esti megiston.
sentences.l:
And the gods to their session were taking their seats, and among them
Zeus the high-thundering, whose might is greatest.
sentences.i: And the gods were taking their seats in session, Zeus who thunders on high among them, whose might is greatest of all.
sentences.n: θῶκόνδε has the directional suffix -δε, 'to the sitting-place'. καθίζανον is an iterative-looking imperfect of καθίζω, 'take a seat'. ὑψιβρεμέτης, 'high-thundering' (ὑψι- 'on high' + βρέμω 'roar, thunder'), is new to this part and kept distinct from the already-fixed εὐρύοπα Ζεύς 'far-thundering Zeus', a different compound. οὗ τε κράτος ἐστὶ μέγιστον, 'whose might is greatest', is a relative clause with the generalizing epic τε, asserting Zeus's primacy among the gods gathered here.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δ’ Ἀθηναίη λέγε κήδεα πόλλ’ Ὀδυσῆος
μνησαμένη·
sentences.tr:
toisi d’ Athēnaiē lege kēdea poll’ Odysēos
mnēsamenē·
sentences.l:
And to them Athena told the many cares of Odysseus,
having called him to mind;
sentences.i: And Athena told them of the many cares of Odysseus, calling him to mind;
sentences.n: λέγε is imperfect of λέγω in its old sense 'tell over, recount', not yet 'say' in the later prose sense. κήδεα, 'cares, troubles', is a plural noun; πόλλ’ is πολλά. μνησαμένη is an aorist participle of μιμνήσκομαι with the genitive Ὀδυσῆος, 'having thought of Odysseus'. This narrator's summary stands before Athena's own words begin at line 7.

sentences.t: μέλε γάρ οἱ ἐὼν ἐν δώμασι νύμφης·
sentences.tr: mele gar hoi eōn en dōmasi nymphēs·
sentences.l: for he was a care to her, being in the halls of the nymph;
sentences.i: for she was troubled that he was still in the halls of the nymph;
sentences.n: μέλε is an unaugmented aorist of μέλω, 'to be a care to (someone)', with the dative οἱ 'to her' (Attic ἔμελε). ἐών is the present participle of εἰμί (Attic ὤν). νύμφης, unnamed here, is of course Calypso, already introduced in Book 1; the narrator assumes the audience remembers her.

sentences.t:
Ζεῦ πάτερ ἠδ’ ἄλλοι μάκαρες θεοὶ αἰὲν ἐόντες,
μή τις ἔτι πρόφρων ἀγανὸς καὶ ἤπιος ἔστω
σκηπτοῦχος βασιλεύς, μηδὲ φρεσὶν αἴσιμα εἰδώς,
ἀλλ’ αἰεὶ χαλεπός τ’ εἴη καὶ αἴσυλα ῥέζοι·
sentences.tr:
Zeu pater ēd’ alloi makares theoi aien eontes,
mē tis eti prophrōn aganos kai ēpios estō
skēptouchos basileus, mēde phresin aisima eidōs,
all’ aiei chalepos t’ eiē kai aisyla rhezoi·
sentences.i: “Father Zeus, and you other blessed gods who are forever — let no sceptred king any longer be ready-minded, gentle and kind, nor mindful of what is right — let him always be harsh and act wickedly instead —
sentences.n: This vocative opening overlaps the already-fixed formula θεοὶ αἰὲν ἐόντες, 'the gods who are forever', expanded here with Ζεῦ πάτερ and μάκαρες 'blessed'. Line 7 ends with a comma, not a full stop, and the wish that follows, μή τις ἔτι πρόφρων … ῥέζοι·, already stood word for word in an earlier part with the same report of a forgotten king; the same English is kept here. The span reaches only four lines before its first full stop, at ῥέζοι· in line 10, so it stands as one tap-unit rather than being cut early. Athena turns to the particular case, Odysseus, next.

sentences.t:
ὡς οὔ τις μέμνηται Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο
λαῶν οἷσιν ἄνασσε, πατὴρ δ’ ὣς ἤπιος ἦεν.
sentences.tr:
hōs ou tis memnētai Odyssēos theioio
laōn hoisin anasse, patēr d’ hōs ēpios ēen.
sentences.l:
as no one remembers divine Odysseus
among the people whom he ruled — and like a father kind he was.
sentences.i: since no one remembers divine Odysseus, among the people he ruled — and was as gentle as a father.
sentences.n: These two lines already stood, word for word, in an earlier part, and the same English is kept here. θείοιο is a genitive in -οιο; θεῖος 'divine' is kept distinct from the already-fixed δῖος 'heavenly' and θεοειδής 'godlike in form', separate epithet-families for Odysseus.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὁ μὲν ἐν νήσῳ κεῖται κρατέρ’ ἄλγεα πάσχων
νύμφης ἐν μεγάροισι Καλυψοῦς, ἥ μιν ἀνάγκῃ
ἴσχει·
sentences.tr:
all’ ho men en nēsōi keitai krater’ algea paschōn
nymphēs en megaroisi Kalypsous, hē min anankēi
ischei·
sentences.i: but he lies on the island suffering harsh pains, in the halls of the nymph Calypso, who holds him there against his will;
sentences.n: The second and third lines here are identical to two lines already published elsewhere, where they described this same situation from another speaker's mouth, and their wording is kept. κεῖται, literally 'lies', is used loosely of a settled, ongoing state, not only of the dead. κρατέρ’ ἄλγεα is κρατερά, 'mighty, harsh', with elision.

sentences.t: ὁ δ’ οὐ δύναται ἣν πατρίδα γαῖαν ἱκέσθαι·
sentences.tr: ho d’ ou dynatai hēn patrida gaian hikesthai·
sentences.l: but he is not able his own fatherland to reach;
sentences.i: and he cannot reach his own native land;
sentences.n: ἣν πατρίδα γαῖαν, 'his own fatherland', uses the possessive ὅς, ἥ, ὅν again, easily mistaken for the relative. The noun-phrase πατρίδα γαῖαν recurs four times in this part (here, 26, 37, 42); at 26, 37 and 42 the i layer gives 'fatherland', but this very line already stands word for word in odyssey-019 (line 4.475), so its i layer here keeps that line's own wording, 'native land', unchanged, as the house rule for an exact repeat requires.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ οἱ πάρα νῆες ἐπήρετμοι καὶ ἑταῖροι,
οἵ κέν μιν πέμποιεν ἐπ’ εὐρέα νῶτα θαλάσσης.
sentences.tr:
ou gar hoi para nēes epēretmoi kai hetairoi,
hoi ken min pempoien ep’ eurea nōta thalassēs.
sentences.l:
For he has no oared ships nor companions,
who might send him over the broad back of the sea.
sentences.i: for he has no oared ships or companions who might convey him over the sea's broad back.
sentences.n: These two lines already stood, word for word, in an earlier part, and the same English is kept here. πάρα is πάρεστι in tmesis-like position, 'are at hand to him'. ἐπήρετμοι, 'oared, fitted with oars', describes ships ready for a sea-voyage, which Odysseus now entirely lacks.

sentences.t:
νῦν αὖ παῖδ’ ἀγαπητὸν ἀποκτεῖναι μεμάασιν
οἴκαδε νισόμενον·
sentences.tr:
nyn au paid’ agapēton apokteinai memaasin
oikade nisomenon·
sentences.l:
And now again his beloved son they are eager to kill,
as he returns homeward;
sentences.i: and now, besides, they are bent on killing his beloved son as he makes his way home;
sentences.n: The subject of μεμάασιν, 'are eager', is left unnamed — the suitors, whose plot against Telemachus the audience already knows from earlier books. μεμάασιν is a perfect with present force. νισόμενον is a present participle of νίσομαι, 'go, return', built on the same root as νόστος. ἀγαπητός marks an only or especially cherished child.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἔβη μετὰ πατρὸς ἀκουὴν
ἐς Πύλον ἠγαθέην ἠδ’ ἐς Λακεδαίμονα δῖαν.
sentences.tr:
ho d’ ebē meta patros akouēn
es Pylon ēgatheēn ēd’ es Lakedaimona dian.
sentences.l:
but he had gone, in quest of news of his father,
to holy Pylos and to heavenly Lacedaemon.”
sentences.i: but he had gone in search of news of his father, to holy Pylos and to heavenly Lacedaemon.”
sentences.n: This line is identical, word for word, to one already published elsewhere, and the same English, including its closing quotation mark, is kept here, since it likewise closes a speech. μετὰ πατρὸς ἀκουήν, 'after news of his father', uses μετά with the accusative of the thing sought. ἠγαθέην is 'very holy', an intensive compound.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ apameibomenos prosephē nephelēgereta Zeus·
sentences.l: Her answering addressed cloud-gatherer Zeus:
sentences.i: In answer Zeus who gathers the clouds said to her:
sentences.n: This line is identical, word for word, to one already published elsewhere, and the same English is kept here. It is the second of the poem's two fixed formulas of reply built on a participle and a form of φημί; τήν is the pronoun 'her'.

sentences.t: τέκνον ἐμόν, ποῖόν σε ἔπος φύγεν ἕρκος ὀδόντων.
sentences.tr: teknon emon, poion se epos phygen herkos odontōn.
sentences.l: “My child, what a word has escaped you, the fence of your teeth.
sentences.i: “My child, what a word is this that has got past the fence of your teeth!
sentences.n: This line is identical, word for word, to one already published elsewhere — Zeus's standing formula of mild rebuke to Athena — and the same English is kept here. φύγεν, unaugmented, takes two objects, σε and ἕρκος, the construction of the whole and the part.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ δὴ τοῦτον μὲν ἐβούλευσας νόον αὐτή,
ὡς ἦ τοι κείνους Ὀδυσεὺς ἀποτίσεται ἐλθών;
sentences.tr:
ou gar dē touton men ebouleusas noon autē,
hōs ē toi keinous Odyseus apotisetai elthōn;
sentences.l:
For did you not indeed yourself devise this very purpose,
that Odysseus, on his coming, would make those men pay?
sentences.i: Did you not yourself devise this very plan, that Odysseus should come home and make those men pay?
sentences.n: οὐ in a question expects the answer 'yes'; δή adds emphasis, 'indeed'. αὐτή, 'yourself', is intensive, stressing that Athena is the plan's own author. κείνους, 'those men', looks back to the suitors just named by Athena. ἀποτίσεται is a future middle of ἀποτίνω, the same verb used of Aegisthus's reckoning in Book 1.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχον δὲ σὺ πέμψον ἐπισταμένως, δύνασαι γάρ,
ὥς κε μάλ’ ἀσκηθὴς ἣν πατρίδα γαῖαν ἵκηται,
μνηστῆρες δ’ ἐν νηὶ·
sentences.tr:
Tēlemachon de sy pempson epistamenōs, dynasai gar,
hōs ke mal’ askēthēs hēn patrida gaian hikētai,
mnēstēres d’ en nēi·
sentences.l:
But send Telemachus off with skill — you are able —
so that quite unharmed he may reach his own fatherland,
and the suitors, in their ship,
sentences.i: But send Telemachus off with skill, since you have the power to, so that he may reach his own fatherland quite unharmed, while the suitors, in their ship,
sentences.n: ἐπισταμένως, 'skilfully, knowingly', is an adverb from ἐπίσταμαι. δύνασαι γάρ, 'for you are able', is a parenthetical aside. ἀσκηθής, 'unharmed', is a compound with the same privative ἀ- as ἀτρύγετος. The edition prints an ano teleia after νηὶ, an unusual mid-line pause; the unit is cut there exactly, and the wish it interrupts is completed in the next unit.

sentences.t: παλιμπετὲς ἀπονέωνται.
sentences.tr: palimpetes aponeōntai.
sentences.l: may they turn back the way they came.”
sentences.i: may turn back the way they came.”
sentences.n: παλιμπετές, 'back again, backward', is an adverb built on πάλιν; ἀπονέωνται is a present subjunctive of ἀπονέομαι, continuing the purpose clause ὥς κε from the line before. The wish is that the suitors' ambush, already narrated in an earlier part, will fail and send them home empty-handed, though Zeus does not spell that out.

sentences.t: ἦ ῥα καὶ Ἑρμείαν, υἱὸν φίλον, ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: ē rha kai Hermeian, huion philon, antion ēuda·
sentences.l: He spoke, and to Hermes too, his dear son, he spoke face to face:
sentences.i: So he said, and then turned to speak to Hermes, his own dear son, face to face:
sentences.n: ἦ ῥα is the same fixed speech-closing phrase seen elsewhere, here combined with καί to mark that a second address follows at once. ἀντίον ηὔδα, 'spoke facing him', is the same verb-phrase already fixed in several reply-formulas naming other speakers, here used of Zeus turning from Athena to Hermes, his son by Maia, within the same scene.

sentences.t:
Ἑρμεία, σὺ γὰρ αὖτε τά τ’ ἄλλα περ ἄγγελός ἐσσι,
νύμφῃ ἐυπλοκάμῳ εἰπεῖν νημερτέα βουλήν,
νόστον Ὀδυσσῆος ταλασίφρονος, ὥς κε νέηται
οὔτε θεῶν πομπῇ οὔτε θνητῶν ἀνθρώπων·
sentences.tr:
Hermeia, sy gar aute ta t’ alla per angelos essi,
nymphēi eyplokamōi eipein nēmertea boulēn,
noston Odyssēos talasiphronos, hōs ke neētai
oute theōn pompēi oute thnētōn anthrōpōn·
sentences.l:
“Hermes, since you, again, in other matters too, are our messenger,
to the fine-plaited nymph tell our unerring decision,
the homecoming of Odysseus the enduring-minded, that he is to return,
neither by the convoy of gods nor of mortal men;
sentences.i: “Hermes — since you are, as in other matters, our messenger — go and tell the nymph of the fine-plaited hair our unfailing decision: the homecoming of steadfast Odysseus, that he is to return, neither with the escort of gods nor of mortal men;
sentences.n: ἐσσι is the epic second-singular of εἰμί. εἰπεῖν is an infinitive standing for an imperative, 'go and tell'. The third line here, νόστον Ὀδυσσῆος ταλασίφρονος, ὥς κε νέηται, is identical to one already published elsewhere and its wording is reused; ταλασίφρων is the third of Odysseus's three -φρων epithets, already fixed as 'enduring-minded' / 'steadfast'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅ γ’ ἐπὶ σχεδίης πολυδέσμου πήματα πάσχων
ἤματί κ’ εἰκοστῷ Σχερίην ἐρίβωλον ἵκοιτο,
Φαιήκων ἐς γαῖαν, οἳ ἀγχίθεοι γεγάασιν,
οἵ κέν μιν περὶ κῆρι θεὸν ὣς τιμήσουσιν,
sentences.tr:
all’ ho g’ epi schediēs polydesmou pēmata paschōn
ēmati k’ eikostōi Scheriēn eribōlon hikoito,
Phaiēkōn es gaian, hoi anchitheoi gegaasin,
hoi ken min peri kēri theon hōs timēsousin,
sentences.l:
but he, upon a raft of many bonds suffering hardships,
on the twentieth day may come to rich-clodded Scheria,
to the land of the Phaeacians, who are close to the gods,
who will honor him in their hearts as a god,
sentences.i: but let him, suffering hardships on his raft of many lashings, reach rich-soiled Scheria on the twentieth day, the land of the Phaeacians, who are close to the gods and will honor him in their hearts as though he were one,
sentences.n: σχεδίη, 'raft', named here for the first time, is the vessel on which Zeus's own speech says Odysseus will make his crossing; πολυδέσμου, 'of many bonds', describes how it is lashed together rather than built with joints. Σχερίη ἐρίβωλος, 'rich-clodded Scheria', and Φαίηκες ἀγχίθεοι, 'the Phaeacians, close to the gods', are both new to the poem here and fixed for their frequent recurrence through the following books.

sentences.t:
πέμψουσιν δ’ ἐν νηὶ φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν,
χαλκόν τε χρυσόν τε ἅλις ἐσθῆτά τε δόντες,
πόλλ’, ὅσ’ ἂν οὐδέ ποτε Τροίης ἐξήρατ’ Ὀδυσσεύς,
εἴ περ ἀπήμων ἦλθε, λαχὼν ἀπὸ ληίδος αἶσαν.
sentences.tr:
pempsousin d’ en nēi philēn es patrida gaian,
chalkon te chryson te halis esthēta te dontes,
poll’, hos’ an oude pote Troiēs exērat’ Odysseus,
ei per apēmōn ēlthe, lachōn apo lēidos aisan.
sentences.l:
and they will send him in a ship to his dear fatherland,
bronze and gold in abundance, and clothing, giving,
much, such as never even from Troy would Odysseus have carried off,
even if unharmed he had come, having taken his share of the spoil.
sentences.i: and will send him by ship to his dear fatherland, giving him bronze and gold in plenty, and clothing — more than Odysseus would ever have carried off from Troy itself, even if he had come home unharmed with his full share of the spoil.
sentences.n: φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν keeps 'his dear fatherland', parallel to the already-fixed φίλη πατρὶς αἶα. ἐξήρατ(ο) is an aorist middle of ἐξαίρω, 'carry off for oneself'. λαχὼν ἀπὸ ληίδος αἶσαν, 'having got his portion from the plunder', pictures the regular division of war-spoil among the Achaean host at Troy.

sentences.t:
ὣς γάρ οἱ μοῖρ’ ἐστὶ φίλους τ’ ἰδέειν καὶ ἱκέσθαι
οἶκον ἐς ὑψόροφον καὶ ἑὴν ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν.
sentences.tr:
hōs gar hoi moir’ esti philous t’ ideein kai hikesthai
oikon es hypsorophon kai heēn es patrida gaian.
sentences.l:
for so it is his portion, his dear ones to see, and to reach
his high-roofed house, and his own fatherland.”
sentences.i: for it is his fate to see his dear ones again, and reach his high-roofed home and his own fatherland.”
sentences.n: μοῖρ(α) ἐστί, 'it is his portion', names what is allotted to a man by fate; the same root gives the already-fixed μοῖρ’ ὀλοή, 'the deadly fate'. ἑήν is a by-form of the possessive ἥν. ὑψόροφον, 'high-roofed', is a distinct compound from the already-fixed ὑψερεφές, 'high-roofed' of Menelaus's hall, but the same plain English serves both. This closes Zeus's speech to Hermes.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε διάκτορος ἀργεϊφόντης.
sentences.tr: hōs ephat’, oud’ apithēse diaktoros argeïphontēs.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and did not disobey the guide, Argeïphontes.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the guide, the slayer of Argus, did not disobey.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ(ο) keeps the fixed speech-closing formula. ἀπίθησε, negated by οὐδέ, is an aorist of ἀπιθέω, 'disobey' (from πείθομαι); the litotes 'did not disobey' marks instant, unquestioning compliance, appropriate to Hermes as Zeus's messenger. διάκτορος ἀργεϊφόντης combines two already-fixed epithets of Hermes, each of disputed or unknown meaning, kept together here as elsewhere.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκ’ ἔπειθ’ ὑπὸ ποσσὶν ἐδήσατο καλὰ πέδιλα,
ἀμβρόσια χρύσεια, τά μιν φέρον ἠμὲν ἐφ’ ὑγρὴν
ἠδ’ ἐπ’ ἀπείρονα γαῖαν ἅμα πνοιῇς ἀνέμοιο.
sentences.tr:
autik’ epeith’ hypo possin edēsato kala pedila,
ambrosia chryseia, ta min pheron ēmen eph’ hygrēn
ēd’ ep’ apeirona gaian hama pnoiēis anemoio.
sentences.l:
Then at once beneath his feet he bound his fair sandals,
immortal, golden, which used to bear him both over the water
and over the boundless earth, together with the breaths of the wind.
sentences.i: Then at once he bound beneath his feet his fair sandals, immortal and golden, which bore him over the water and over the boundless earth alike, keeping pace with the breath of the wind.
sentences.n: The last two lines here are identical to two lines already published elsewhere, of Athena binding the same sandals; that wording is reused, with the pronouns changed from feminine to masculine since Hermes, not Athena, wears them here. This opening line differs from the earlier one only in its first words, αὐτίκ’ ἔπειθ’, 'then at once', in place of ὣς εἰποῦσ’, 'so having spoken'.

sentences.t:
εἵλετο δὲ ῥάβδον, τῇ τ’ ἀνδρῶν ὄμματα θέλγει,
ὧν ἐθέλει, τοὺς δ’ αὖτε καὶ ὑπνώοντας ἐγείρει.
sentences.tr:
heileto de rhabdon, tēi t’ andrōn ommata thelgei,
hōn ethelei, tous d’ aute kai hypnōontas egeirei.
sentences.l:
And he took up his wand, with which the eyes of men he charms,
of whomever he wishes, and others again, even sleeping, he wakes.
sentences.i: And he took up his wand, with which he charms the eyes of whatever men he wishes, and wakes others again even out of sleep.
sentences.n: ῥάβδος, 'wand, rod', is Hermes's standing attribute, the same object named again at line 87 by the epithet χρυσόρραπι, 'of the golden wand'. θέλγει is the verb already met of Calypso's own enchanting speech in Book 1; here it is Hermes's wand, rather than speech, that has the power to lull or rouse the eyes of mortals.

sentences.t: τὴν μετὰ χερσὶν ἔχων πέτετο κρατὺς ἀργεϊφόντης.
sentences.tr: tēn meta chersin echōn peteto kratys argeïphontēs.
sentences.l: This in his hands holding, flew the strong Argeïphontes.
sentences.i: Holding this in his hands, the strong slayer of Argus flew on his way.
sentences.n: τήν is the pronoun 'it', the wand just named. πέτετο is an unaugmented imperfect of πέτομαι, 'fly'. κρατύς, 'strong, mighty', is a plain adjective here, not itself a fixed formula, paired with the already-fixed ἀργεϊφόντης, 'Argeïphontes' / 'the slayer of Argus', whose meaning remains disputed.

sentences.t: Πιερίην δ’ ἐπιβὰς ἐξ αἰθέρος ἔμπεσε πόντῳ·
sentences.tr: Pieriēn d’ epibas ex aitheros empese pontōi·
sentences.l: And having stepped down at Pieria, from the upper air he fell upon the sea;
sentences.i: and touching down at Pieria, he swooped from the upper air onto the sea;
sentences.n: Πιερίη is a region on the northern edge of Olympus, sacred in later legend to the Muses; it is named here only as a landmark on Hermes's flightpath down from heaven. ἐπιβάς is an aorist participle of ἐπιβαίνω, 'step upon, alight'. αἰθήρ is the bright upper air, as opposed to the lower ἀήρ, mist or haze.

sentences.t:
σεύατ’ ἔπειτ’ ἐπὶ κῦμα λάρῳ ὄρνιθι ἐοικώς,
ὅς τε κατὰ δεινοὺς κόλπους ἁλὸς ἀτρυγέτοιο
ἰχθῦς ἀγρώσσων πυκινὰ πτερὰ δεύεται ἅλμῃ·
sentences.tr:
seuat’ epeit’ epi kyma larōi ornithi eoikōs,
hos te kata deinous kolpous halos atrygetoio
ichthys agrōssōn pykina ptera deuetai halmēi·
sentences.i: then he sped out over the waves, in the likeness of a gull that, hunting fish along the dread gulfs of the sea that yields no harvest, wets its thick wings in the brine;
sentences.n: σεύατ(ο) is an unaugmented aorist middle of σεύω, 'dart, rush'. λάρῳ ὄρνιθι ἐοικώς, 'like a gull, a bird', is a new simile-formula, its two nouns in apposition before the participle 'being like'; it is kept literal, with 'bird' retained rather than dropped, since ἐοικώς governs the whole phrase. ἁλὸς ἀτρυγέτοιο keeps the already-fixed 'of the unharvested salt-sea'.

sentences.t: τῷ ἴκελος πολέεσσιν ὀχήσατο κύμασιν Ἑρμῆς.
sentences.tr: tōi ikelos poleessin ochēsato kymasin Hermēs.
sentences.l: like to it, over many waves rode Hermes.
sentences.i: like the gull, Hermes rode on over the many waves.
sentences.n: τῷ ἴκελος, 'like to it', points back to the gull of the simile just given. πολέεσσι is an uncontracted dative plural of πολύς (Attic πολλοῖς). ὀχήσατο is an aorist middle of ὀχέομαι, 'be borne, ride'. The god's own bare name, Ἑρμῆς, closes the line — the plain form beside the fuller Ἑρμείας used elsewhere in this part.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ τὴν νῆσον ἀφίκετο τηλόθ’ ἐοῦσαν,
ἔνθ’ ἐκ πόντου βὰς ἰοειδέος ἤπειρόνδε
ἤιεν, ὄφρα μέγα σπέος ἵκετο, τῷ ἔνι νύμφη
ναῖεν ἐυπλόκαμος·
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē tēn nēson aphiketo tēloth’ eousan,
enth’ ek pontou bas ioeideos ēpeironde
ēien, ophra mega speos hiketo, tōi eni nymphē
naien eyplokamos·
sentences.l:
But when indeed he reached the island, lying far off,
there, stepping from the violet-dark sea onto the mainland,
he went, until he came to the great cave, where the nymph
of the fine-plaited hair dwelt;
sentences.i: But when he reached the island, far off as it lay, he stepped from the violet-dark sea onto the mainland there and walked on until he came to the great cave where the fine-plaited nymph made her home;
sentences.n: ἰοειδέος, 'violet-dark', built on ἴον 'violet', is a fourth distinct sea-colour epithet in the poem, kept apart from the already-fixed οἶνοψ 'wine-faced', πολιή 'grey' and ἠεροειδής 'misty-looking'. ἤπειρόνδε has the directional suffix -δε, 'to the mainland'. ἐυπλόκαμος, 'fine-plaited', is Calypso's own standing epithet, already used of her in this same wording at line 30.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἔνδοθι τέτμεν ἐοῦσαν.
sentences.tr: tēn d’ endothi tetmen eousan.
sentences.l: and her within he found being present.
sentences.i: and found her there inside.
sentences.n: τέτμεν is an unaugmented aorist of a defective verb 'find, come upon' (Attic ἔτυχε would not serve; this is a distinct root). ἐοῦσαν, the present participle of εἰμί agreeing with τήν, adds little beyond 'there', a common Homeric pleonasm with verbs of finding.

sentences.t:
πῦρ μὲν ἐπ’ ἐσχαρόφιν μέγα καίετο, τηλόσε δ’ ὀδμὴ
κέδρου τ’ εὐκεάτοιο θύου τ’ ἀνὰ νῆσον ὀδώδει
δαιομένων·
sentences.tr:
pyr men ep’ escharophin mega kaieto, tēlose d’ odmē
kedrou t’ eukeatoio thyou t’ ana nēson odōdei
daiomenōn·
sentences.i: A great fire was burning on the hearth, and the fragrance of split cedar and citron-wood, as they burned, spread far across the island;
sentences.n: ἐσχαρόφιν has the instrumental-locative suffix -φι(ν), 'at the hearth'. εὐκεάτοιο, 'easily-split', describes cedar cut for burning. θύου, from θύον, is a fragrant wood, conventionally 'citron-wood' or thyine wood, though the exact identity of the ancient tree is not certain. ὀδώδει is a pluperfect-with-imperfect-sense of ὄζω, 'smell of'.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ ἔνδον ἀοιδιάουσ’ ὀπὶ καλῇ
ἱστὸν ἐποιχομένη χρυσείῃ κερκίδ’ ὕφαινεν.
sentences.tr:
hē d’ endon aoidiaous’ opi kalēi
histon epoichomenē chryseiēi kerkid’ hyphainen.
sentences.l:
and she within, singing with a beautiful voice,
plying the loom, with a golden shuttle wove.
sentences.i: and inside, singing in a beautiful voice, she moved back and forth at her loom, weaving with a golden shuttle.
sentences.n: ἀοιδιάουσα is a present participle with the diminutive-frequentative suffix -ιάω, 'singing (as she works)'. ὀπί is the dative of ὄψ, 'voice'. ἱστὸν ἐποιχομένη, 'going to and fro at the loom', pictures the weaver passing the shuttle across the warp; κερκίς is the shuttle itself, here golden, a mark of Calypso's divine housekeeping.

sentences.t:
ὕλη δὲ σπέος ἀμφὶ πεφύκει τηλεθόωσα,
κλήθρη τ’ αἴγειρός τε καὶ εὐώδης κυπάρισσος.
sentences.tr:
hylē de speos amphi pephykei tēlethoōsa,
klēthrē t’ aigeiros te kai euōdēs kyparissos.
sentences.l:
And a wood around the cave had grown, flourishing,
alder and poplar and fragrant cypress.
sentences.i: Round about the cave a flourishing wood had grown up — alder, poplar, and fragrant cypress.
sentences.n: πεφύκει is a pluperfect-with-imperfect-sense of φύω, 'grow, come to be'. τηλεθόωσα is a present participle with the vowel stretched out (diectasis), 'flourishing'. The three named trees — κλήθρη alder, αἴγειρος poplar, κυπάρισσος cypress — are ordinary, recognisable species, unlike the disputed θύον of line 60.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δέ τ’ ὄρνιθες τανυσίπτεροι εὐνάζοντο,
σκῶπές τ’ ἴρηκές τε τανύγλωσσοί τε κορῶναι
εἰνάλιαι, τῇσίν τε θαλάσσια ἔργα μέμηλεν.
sentences.tr:
entha de t’ ornithes tanysipteroi eunazonto,
skōpes t’ irēkes te tanyglōssoi te korōnai
einaliai, tēisin te thalassia erga memēlen.
sentences.l:
There long-winged birds were roosting,
horned owls and falcons and long-tongued crows,
sea-crows, whose care is the works of the sea.
sentences.i: There long-winged birds roosted — horned owls, falcons, and long-tongued sea-crows, whose business is with the sea.
sentences.n: The exact species behind σκῶπες, 'small owls', and the 'sea-crows' εἰνάλιαι κορῶναι (likely a kind of cormorant or shag) are not certainly identifiable from the Greek alone. τανύγλωσσοι, 'long-tongued', is a curious epithet for crows, perhaps referring to their harsh, drawn-out cry. μέμηλεν is a perfect of μέλω, 'is a care to', with the dative τῇσιν.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ αὐτοῦ τετάνυστο περὶ σπείους γλαφυροῖο
ἡμερὶς ἡβώωσα, τεθήλει δὲ σταφυλῇσι.
sentences.tr:
hē d’ autou tetanysto peri speious glaphyroio
hēmeris hēbōōsa, tethēlei de staphylēisi.
sentences.l:
And there, right there, was stretched around the hollow cave
a cultivated vine, in its bloom, and it flourished with clusters.
sentences.i: And right there, around the hollow cave, a garden vine spread in full bloom, rich with clusters of grapes.
sentences.n: τετάνυστο is a pluperfect passive of τανύω, 'stretch, spread'. ἡμερίς, 'cultivated vine' (from ἥμερος 'tame', as against wild ἄγριος), is distinguished from a wild grapevine; ἡβώωσα, 'in its youthful bloom', and τεθήλει, 'was flourishing', both stress the vine's vigor and fruitfulness even in this supernatural, unfarmed place.

sentences.t:
κρῆναι δ’ ἑξείης πίσυρες ῥέον ὕδατι λευκῷ,
πλησίαι ἀλλήλων τετραμμέναι ἄλλυδις ἄλλη.
sentences.tr:
krēnai d’ hexeiēs pisyres rheon hydati leukōi,
plēsiai allēlōn tetrammenai allydis allē.
sentences.l:
And springs, four in a row, were flowing with bright water,
close to one another, turned each a different way.
sentences.i: Four springs, set in a row, flowed with clear water, close to one another, each one turned a different way.
sentences.n: πίσυρες is an Aeolic-epic form of τέσσαρες, 'four'. ῥέον is an unaugmented imperfect of ῥέω, 'flow'. ἄλλυδις ἄλλη, 'one this way, another that', is a reduplicated adverbial idiom meaning 'in different directions'. This passage, with its trees, vine and springs, is among the most famous landscape descriptions in the poem.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δὲ λειμῶνες μαλακοὶ ἴου ἠδὲ σελίνου
θήλεον.
sentences.tr:
amphi de leimōnes malakoi iou ēde selinou
thēleon.
sentences.l:
and round about, soft meadows of violet and of parsley
were blooming.
sentences.i: and all around, soft meadows of violets and wild celery were in bloom.
sentences.n: λειμῶνες μαλακοί, 'soft meadows', pairs the meadow-word with an adjective usually applied to a person's skin or a bed; here it suggests grass soft underfoot. σέλινον is more precisely wild celery than the garden herb later called parsley. θήλεον is an unaugmented imperfect of θηλέω, 'bloom, flourish' — a distinct, root-cognate byform of θάλλω, not that verb's own imperfect — echoing τεθήλει, the pluperfect-as-imperfect of θάλλω itself, at line 69.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα κ’ ἔπειτα καὶ ἀθάνατός περ ἐπελθὼν
θηήσαιτο ἰδὼν καὶ τερφθείη φρεσὶν ᾗσιν.
sentences.tr:
entha k’ epeita kai athanatos per epelthōn
thēēsaito idōn kai terphtheiē phresin hēisin.
sentences.l:
There then even one immortal, though he be, coming upon it,
might gaze in wonder, seeing it, and delight in his own heart.
sentences.i: There even a god, coming upon the place, might well stand and marvel at the sight, and take delight in his heart.
sentences.n: The narrator steps outside the story to remark that even a god would be struck by the scene — and the next line shows exactly that happening to Hermes. ἀθάνατός περ, 'immortal though he be', uses περ concessively with a noun rather than a participle. θηήσαιτο and τερφθείη are both optatives of a general potential, 'would' or 'might'.

sentences.t: ἔνθα στὰς θηεῖτο διάκτορος ἀργεϊφόντης.
sentences.tr: entha stas thēeito diaktoros argeïphontēs.
sentences.l: There standing, gazed in wonder the guide, Argeïphontes.
sentences.i: There the guide, the slayer of Argus, stood and gazed in wonder.
sentences.n: στάς is the aorist participle of ἵστημι, 'having stood'. θηεῖτο is an imperfect of θηέομαι, 'gaze at, marvel at', the same verb just used twice of the god who 'might' marvel; Hermes, arriving, does exactly what the general reflection predicted. διάκτορος ἀργεϊφόντης keeps its fixed rendering.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δὴ πάντα ἑῷ θηήσατο θυμῷ,
αὐτίκ’ ἄρ’ εἰς εὐρὺ σπέος ἤλυθεν.
sentences.tr:
autar epei dē panta heōi thēēsato thymōi,
autik’ ar’ eis eury speos ēlythen.
sentences.l:
But when indeed all things in his own heart he had wondered at,
at once then into the wide cave he went.
sentences.i: But when he had taken in the whole sight to his heart's content, he went at once into the wide cave.
sentences.n: ἑῷ is the possessive ἑός, 'his own' (= ὅς, ἥ, ὅν), agreeing with θυμῷ. θηήσατο is the aorist middle of the same verb θηέομαι just seen in the imperfect. ἤλυθεν is an augmented aorist of ἔρχομαι on the epic root ἐλυθ- (with epenthetic -υ-): the initial ε lengthens to η under the regular temporal augment, exactly as with ὤρνυθ’ at line 1 and ἦσθε at line 94; the Attic equivalent is ἦλθεν, itself likewise augmented, from the parallel shorter root ἐλθ- (whose bare, unaugmented stem shows in the infinitive ἐλθεῖν and the participle ἐλθών).

sentences.t:
οὐδέ μιν ἄντην
ἠγνοίησεν ἰδοῦσα Καλυψώ, δῖα θεάων·
sentences.tr:
oude min antēn
ēgnoiēsen idousa Kalypsō, dia theaōn·
sentences.l:
Nor him, face to face,
failed to recognize, seeing him, Calypso, heavenly-one of goddesses;
sentences.i: and Calypso, heavenly even among goddesses, did not fail to know him the moment she saw him face to face;
sentences.n: ἄντην, 'face to face, opposite', modifies the whole clause. ἠγνοίησεν, negated by οὐδέ, is an aorist of ἀγνοέω, 'fail to recognize, not know'; the litotes stresses that gods recognize one another instantly, a point the next two lines make explicit. δῖα θεάων keeps its already-fixed rendering, 'heavenly-one of goddesses' / 'heavenly even among goddesses'.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ τ’ ἀγνῶτες θεοὶ ἀλλήλοισι πέλονται
ἀθάνατοι, οὐδ’ εἴ τις ἀπόπροθι δώματα ναίει.
sentences.tr:
ou gar t’ agnōtes theoi allēloisi pelontai
athanatoi, oud’ ei tis apoprothi dōmata naiei.
sentences.l:
for gods are not unknown to one another,
the immortals, not even if one far off has his dwelling.
sentences.i: for the immortal gods are never strangers to one another, even if one of them lives far away.
sentences.n: ἀγνῶτες, 'unknown', is built on the same privative ἀ- and root γνω- as ἠγνοίησεν just above. πέλονται is a present of πέλομαι, 'be, exist', an epic alternative to εἰμί. This general reflection explains, within the story itself, why Calypso needs no introduction to know that her visitor is Hermes.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρ’ Ὀδυσσῆα μεγαλήτορα ἔνδον ἔτετμεν,
ἀλλ’ ὅ γ’ ἐπ’ ἀκτῆς κλαῖε καθήμενος, ἔνθα πάρος περ,
δάκρυσι καὶ στοναχῇσι καὶ ἄλγεσι θυμὸν ἐρέχθων.
sentences.tr:
oud’ ar’ Odyssēa megalētora endon etetmen,
all’ ho g’ ep’ aktēs klaie kathēmenos, entha paros per,
dakrysi kai stonachēisi kai algesi thymon erechthōn.
sentences.l:
Nor indeed did she find great-spirited Odysseus within,
but he sat weeping on the shore, just as before too,
racking his heart with tears and groans and pains.
sentences.i: But she did not find great-spirited Odysseus inside; he was sitting on the shore, weeping just as he always did, tormenting his heart with tears and groans and pain.
sentences.n: μεγαλήτορα is the same word already fixed elsewhere as 'great-spirited' for a different hero, Telemachus; the same English is kept here for Odysseus, applying the table's own method to a new referent, and the extension is recorded for the conventions file. ἔνθα πάρος περ, 'there, even as before', shows this is Odysseus's daily, habitual place and posture. ἐρέχθων, 'racking, agitating', is a present participle governing θυμόν.

sentences.t: πόντον ἐπ’ ἀτρύγετον δερκέσκετο δάκρυα λείβων.
sentences.tr: ponton ep’ atrygeton derkesketo dakrya leibōn.
sentences.l: Toward the unharvested sea he kept gazing, tears pouring.
sentences.i: He kept gazing out over the sea that yields no harvest, pouring out his tears.
sentences.n: πόντον ἀτρύγετον extends the already-fixed ἁλὸς ἀτρυγέτοιο to the synonym πόντος, 'sea', kept to the same rendering. δερκέσκετο is an iterative imperfect in -σκε, 'kept gazing, would gaze again and again'. δάκρυα λείβων, 'pouring tears', is a new formula, its verb λείβω 'pour, let fall drop by drop' kept distinct from the already-fixed δάκρυ χέων, 'shedding a tear', a different verb.

sentences.t:
Ἑρμείαν δ’ ἐρέεινε Καλυψώ, δῖα θεάων,
ἐν θρόνῳ ἱδρύσασα φαεινῷ σιγαλόεντι·
sentences.tr:
Hermeian d’ ereeine Kalypsō, dia theaōn,
en thronōi hidrysasa phaeinōi sigaloenti·
sentences.l:
Him then questioned Calypso, heavenly-one of goddesses,
having seated him on a shining, gleaming throne;
sentences.i: And Calypso, heavenly even among goddesses, questioned Hermes, after seating him on a bright, gleaming throne;
sentences.n: Ἑρμείαν is the grammatical object, placed first, and Καλυψώ the subject of ἐρέεινε, 'questioned'; the object-first order is kept in l as elsewhere in the poem's reply-formulas. ἱδρύσασα is an aorist participle of ἱδρύω, 'set, seat'. φαεινῷ σιγαλόεντι piles up two near-synonyms for 'shining', marking the throne's splendor as fitting a goddess's hospitality.

sentences.t:
τίπτε μοι, Ἑρμεία χρυσόρραπι, εἰλήλουθας
αἰδοῖός τε φίλος τε;
sentences.tr:
tipte moi, Hermeia chrysorrapi, eilēlouthas
aidoios te philos te;
sentences.l:
“Why, to me, Hermes of the golden wand, have you come,
both honored and dear?
sentences.i: “Why have you come to me, Hermes of the golden wand — honored guest and dear?
sentences.n: χρυσόρραπι, 'of the golden wand', is Hermes's standing epithet, first fixed here and referring to the same ῥάβδος named at line 47. αἰδοῖός τε φίλος τε, 'both honored and dear', a new formula of welcome, joins αἰδοῖος 'deserving respect' (from αἰδώς) with φίλος 'dear'. εἰλήλουθας is a reduplicated perfect of ἔρχομαι, 'you have come (and are here)'.

sentences.t: πάρος γε μὲν οὔ τι θαμίζεις.
sentences.tr: paros ge men ou ti thamizeis.
sentences.l: yet before now you were no frequent visitor.
sentences.i: though you have not made a habit of visiting before now.
sentences.n: θαμίζεις is a present of θαμίζω, 'come often, be a frequent visitor', negated by οὔ τι, 'not at all'. πάρος γε μέν, 'before now, at least', sets the present unusual visit against Hermes's ordinary absence — a courteous way of registering surprise without yet asking his errand directly.

sentences.t: αὔδα ὅ τι φρονέεις·
sentences.tr: auda ho ti phroneeis·
sentences.l: Say what you have in mind;
sentences.i: Tell me what is on your mind;
sentences.n: αὔδα is a present imperative of αὐδάω, 'speak, say'. ὅ τι φρονέεις, 'whatever you are thinking', is an indirect question serving as the object. Calypso moves briskly from her greeting to inviting Hermes's business, though the request that follows still holds off asking outright.

sentences.t:
τελέσαι δέ με θυμὸς ἄνωγεν,
εἰ δύναμαι τελέσαι γε καὶ εἰ τετελεσμένον ἐστίν.
sentences.tr:
telesai de me thymos anōgen,
ei dynamai telesai ge kai ei tetelesmenon estin.
sentences.l:
and to accomplish it my heart bids me,
if I am able to accomplish it, and if it is a thing accomplishable.
sentences.i: and my heart urges me to do it, if I can, and if it is a thing that is meant to be done.
sentences.n: ἄνωγεν is a perfect-with-present-sense of a defective verb, 'bids, commands'. τετελεσμένον ἐστίν, literally 'is a thing brought to fulfillment', likely means not merely 'possible' but 'ordained, fated to happen' — a polite acknowledgment that Hermes may be bringing an order from Zeus that would outweigh her own wishes.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἕπεο προτέρω, ἵνα τοι πὰρ ξείνια θείω.
sentences.tr: all’ hepeo proterō, hina toi par xeinia theiō.
sentences.l: But come further forward, so that for you I may set out gifts of hospitality.”
sentences.i: But come farther in, so that I may set out for you the gifts due a guest.”
sentences.n: ἕπεο is a present imperative of ἕπομαι, here used loosely for 'come along, follow me in'. ξείνια, 'guest-gifts', from ξένος, are the food and courtesies owed to any visitor under the rules of hospitality; θείω is an aorist subjunctive of τίθημι, 'set out, place'. Calypso's own speech is grammatically complete at this line — the narrator's fixed closing formula ὥς ἄρα φωνήσασα follows immediately — even though Hermes does not answer her until after the meal, so the closing quotation mark belongs here rather than later.

sentences.t:
ὥς ἄρα φωνήσασα θεὰ παρέθηκε τράπεζαν
ἀμβροσίης πλήσασα, κέρασσε δὲ νέκταρ ἐρυθρόν.
sentences.tr:
hōs ara phōnēsasa thea parethēke trapezan
ambrosiēs plēsasa, kerasse de nektar erythron.
sentences.l:
So then having spoken, the goddess set beside him a table,
having filled it with ambrosia, and mixed red nectar.
sentences.i: So she spoke, and set a table before him, filled with ambrosia, and mixed him red nectar.
sentences.n: ὥς ἄρα φωνήσασα is the same fixed speech-closing formula already met elsewhere, here unelided before a consonant; its wording, 'So then having spoken,' / 'So she spoke, and', is kept. ἀμβροσία and νέκταρ are the gods' own food and drink; κέρασσε, 'mixed', is the aorist of κεράννυμι, used of mixing wine or nectar with water in due proportion.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ὁ πῖνε καὶ ἦσθε διάκτορος ἀργεϊφόντης.
sentences.tr: autar ho pine kai ēsthe diaktoros argeïphontēs.
sentences.l: Then he drank and ate, the guide, Argeïphontes.
sentences.i: And the guide, the slayer of Argus, ate and drank.
sentences.n: πῖνε is an unaugmented imperfect of πίνω 'drink'; ἦσθε is the imperfect of the old suppletive verb ἔδω 'eat', here showing its regular augment (ε lengthened to η), contrasted with the unaugmented plural ἔδον found elsewhere in Homer. Both describe the meal as it went on rather than as a single completed act. διάκτορος ἀργεϊφόντης again keeps its fixed rendering, closing the line as it closed lines 43 and 75.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δείπνησε καὶ ἤραρε θυμὸν ἐδωδῇ,
καὶ τότε δή μιν ἔπεσσιν ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπεν·
sentences.tr:
autar epei deipnēse kai ērare thymon edōdēi,
kai tote dē min epessin ameibomenos proseeipen·
sentences.l:
But when he had dined, and had fitted his heart with food,
then indeed, with words, answering, he addressed her:
sentences.i: But when he had eaten his fill and satisfied his heart with food, he then answered her, and spoke:
sentences.n: ἤραρε θυμὸν ἐδωδῇ, 'fitted his heart with food', uses the same verb ἀραρίσκω, 'fit, join', already met in the figurative sense 'satisfy'. The closing formula μιν ἔπεσσιν ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπεν combines 'answering' and 'addressed' in one new masculine reply-formula, parallel to an already-fixed feminine one built on the same two verbs; Hermes's actual reply opens the part that follows.
